fieldFixes.contribution: Soltani was the primary technical consultant on The Wall Street Journal's 'What They Know' tracking investigation, Chief Technologist of the US Federal Trade Commission and an architect of California's CCPA and CPRA privacy laws, and his biographies credit him as a co-creator of Do Not Track. In October 2020 he and Sebastian Zimmeck launched Global Privacy Control with publishers, browsers and EFF, a browser setting that tells each site the user opts out of sale or sharing of their data, which California regulations require businesses to honour. On 4 October 2021 he became the first executive director of the California Privacy Protection Agency, serving until January 2025.

fieldFixes.title: 'Komputerfrieks' meet at the taz: the Chaos Computer Club's informal founding
fieldFixes.summary: A notice headed 'TUWAT,TXT Version' in the taz of 1 September 1981, signed by five Hamburg media activists including Wau Holland and Klaus Schleisiek, invited computer enthusiasts to meet at the paper's Wattstraße building on 12 September 1981. Some 20 people are said to have come, meeting at a large table that had once stood in the Kommune 1. The Chaos Computer Club counts this meeting as its informal founding, though the name itself seems to have come into use only around the end of 1982. The notice's topic list included data law under the question 'who owns my data?'.

What officials confirmed (Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann, Monday 10 October 2011) was that the CCC's sample could be traced to a 2009 Bavarian police investigation (Tagesspiegel, Abendzeitung). fieldFixes.summary: On 8 October 2011 the CCC published binaries and an analysis of 'lawful interception' malware used by German police, sent to it anonymously. It reported that software meant only to tap internet telephony could also take screenshots, load and run further programs and be taken over by third parties, because its commands were unencrypted and unauthenticated. The club argued this breached limits set by the Federal Constitutional Court in its 27 February 2008 ruling. Two days later Bavaria's interior ministry confirmed that the sample came from a 2009 Bavarian police investigation, and the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that Bavarian police had used the trojan in five cases.
fieldFixes.significance: Hackers, not a regulator, audited the state's own surveillance code, and argued that a person's computer had become part of the 'core area of private life'.

issues: The summary says 'led a court to hold that e-mail deserves at least as much protection as telephone calls' as if it were the court's holding. That wording is EFF's own gloss from its history page. The actual 12 March 1993 ruling by Judge Sam Sparks (W.D. Tex.) awarded each plaintiff $1,000 under the ECPA for the seizure of their stored e-mail, but 'did not find that Secret Service agents had "intercepted" the electronic communications' (EFFector 5/4, 19 March 1993). The Fifth Circuit upheld that no-interception finding in October 1994, which is the opposite of telephone-call-level (Wiretap Act) protection. The sentence is reworded to state the real holding and attribute the gloss to EFF.

'EFF's first case' is EFF's own label (eff.org/issues/video-games: 'EFF's first case in 1990...'). Barlow's 8 November 1990 history, however, shows EFF's first legal action was a supporting amicus brief for Craig Neidorf, whose prosecution collapsed in late July 1990. The Steve Jackson Games suit was the lawsuit announced at launch. The wording is changed to 'the lawsuit EFF announced at its launch'.

The significance field claims EFF was 'the first advocacy organisation built to argue for privacy and speech rights inside networks'. That is overstated. Barlow's 1990 history records that one of EFF's first acts was a $275,000 grant to Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility's existing Washington office 'for a project on computing and civil liberties'. 'the first' is dropped.

The other claims check out: 1 March 1990 raid (SSIR), stored BBS e-mail 'individually accessed and deleted' (EFF history), the Kapor/Barlow/Gilmore founders, the 10 July 1990 National Press Club announcement (SSIR and Barlow 1990: 'We announced the formation of the Electronic Frontier Foundation at the National Press Club on July 10'), and the founding-paper quote. The locationNote's '155 Second St. Cambridge, MA 02141' is FOUND in Barlow's 8 November 1990 history.

fieldFixes.summary: After a 1 March 1990 Secret Service raid on Steve Jackson Games in Austin, Texas, in which the company's bulletin-board e-mail was accessed and deleted, Mitch Kapor, John Perry Barlow and John Gilmore formed an organisation for civil liberties raised by new technologies. Kapor and Barlow announced the Electronic Frontier Foundation in Washington on 10 July 1990, with a founding paper asking whether 'the history of one's personal business affairs' could properly belong to someone else. The lawsuit EFF announced at its launch, for Steve Jackson Games, ended in a 1993 federal ruling that the seizure of users' stored e-mail violated the Electronic Communications Privacy Act. EFF calls it the first time a court held that e-mail deserves at least as much protection as telephone calls.
fieldFixes.significance: Created an advocacy organisation built specifically to argue for privacy and speech rights inside networks, and framed personal data as something that might belong to the person.
